lesson.title: Making the Quotient Rule Second Nature
lesson.summary: This section drills the quotient rule into a fast, reliable formula, with careful attention to the order of subtraction in the numerator, the most common place students slip up.
lesson.body:
With the quotient rule now derived, it pays to state it as a formula ready for instant use: if q(x) = f(x)/g(x), then q'(x) = [f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x)] / [g(x)]^2. A handy way to remember the order of subtraction is a small rhyme some students use: derivative of the top times the bottom, minus the top times the derivative of the bottom, all over the bottom squared. Getting this order backwards, subtracting in the wrong direction, is the single most common mistake with this rule, and it silently flips the sign of every answer, so it is worth double checking on every problem until the order feels automatic.

A second worked example, chosen to be a little busier than the previous one, helps cement the formula. Let q(x) = (3x - 2)/(x^2 + 5). Here f(x) = 3x - 2 so f'(x) = 3, and g(x) = x^2 + 5 so g'(x) = 2x. Plugging into the formula, q'(x) = [3(x^2+5) - (3x-2)(2x)] / (x^2+5)^2. Expand the numerator piece by piece: 3(x^2+5) = 3x^2 + 15, and (3x-2)(2x) = 6x^2 - 4x. Subtracting gives 3x^2 + 15 - 6x^2 + 4x = -3x^2 + 4x + 15. So q'(x) = (-3x^2 + 4x + 15)/(x^2+5)^2.

Evaluate this at x = 1 as a checkpoint: the numerator becomes -3 + 4 + 15 = 16, and the denominator becomes (1+5)^2 = 36, giving q'(1) = 16/36 = 4/9, which is about 0.444. A quick numerical check backs this up: q(1) = (3-2)/(1+5) = 1/6, about 0.1667, and q(1.01) = (3.03-2)/(1.0201+5) = 1.03/6.0201, about 0.1711. The difference quotient [0.1711 - 0.1667]/0.01 is about 0.44, matching the formula's 4/9 closely, with the small remaining gap again explained by the finite step size rather than any error in the formula.

Two structural facts about the formula are worth noticing once it feels routine. First, the denominator [g(x)]^2 is always positive wherever it is defined, since it is a square, so the sign of the entire derivative is controlled entirely by the numerator f'(x)g(x) - f(x)g'(x). Second, when f(x) is just a constant, the quotient rule should quietly reduce to something simpler, since a constant divided by g(x) is really a constant times 1/g(x). That simplification is exactly the subject of the reciprocal rule, which specializes this same formula to the case of a constant numerator.

It is instructive to see exactly what goes wrong if the subtraction order is flipped by accident. Reversing the terms in the x^2+5 example gives (3x-2)(2x) - 3(x^2+5) = 6x^2 - 4x - 3x^2 - 15 = 3x^2 - 4x - 15, which is precisely the negative of the correct numerator, -3x^2 + 4x + 15. Since the denominator (x^2+5)^2 is unaffected by the swap, the entire derivative would come out with the opposite sign at every single x value, turning a decreasing function into an apparently increasing one or vice versa. This is exactly why the order in derivative of the top times the bottom, minus the top times the derivative of the bottom deserves to be memorized precisely, not approximately.

Practicing the formula on a handful of quick examples, always checking the sign of the subtraction and always squaring the denominator, is the fastest route to using it fluently on more complicated functions later, including trigonometric ratios like tangent and secant, which are themselves built as quotients of sine and cosine.
